title: 📚 Advanced Academic Vocabulary — Set 2

sections.heading: Words that signal academic thinking
sections.body:
Set 2 focuses on words that show CRITICAL THINKING in your writing:

• Words that indicate stance: 'contend', 'assert', 'refute'
• Words that show causation: 'precipitate', 'engender', 'underpin'
• Words that describe change: 'transform', 'reshape', 'erode'
• Words that indicate extent: 'substantially', 'marginally', 'disproportionately'

sections.heading: How to use them
sections.body:
These words don't just describe — they show the examiner you can think analytically.

❌ Basic: 'Technology has changed society a lot.'
✅ Advanced: 'Digital technology has fundamentally reshaped societal structures, engendering both unprecedented connectivity and new forms of inequality.'

highlight: One precise advanced verb ('precipitate', 'engender') is worth more than three simple ones ('cause', 'make', 'lead to'). Precision is the goal.

meaning: to cause something (usually undesirable) to happen suddenly
example: The financial crisis precipitated a wave of unemployment across the region.
wrong: not the same as 'prevent' — it CAUSES, not stops

question: Which sentence uses 'precipitate' correctly?
options: The new law will precipitate the problem of pollution.
Scientists hope to precipitate climate change.
The banking collapse precipitated the worst recession in decades.
Exercise can precipitate good health outcomes.
correct: The banking collapse precipitated the worst recession in decades.
explanation:
'Precipitate' means to CAUSE something negative to happen suddenly.

✅ 'The banking collapse precipitated the recession' — collapse caused (triggered) recession suddenly ✅

❌ 'Precipitate the problem' — you don't precipitate a problem; you precipitate a CRISIS or EVENT
❌ 'Precipitate climate change' — climate change is an ongoing process, not a sudden event
❌ 'Precipitate good health' — precipitate is used for sudden, often negative events
hint: Precipitate suggests suddenness and usually a negative trigger event.

meaning: to cause or give rise to a feeling, situation, or condition
example: The policy engendered widespread resentment among the affected communities.
wrong: not the same as 'gender' — it means to CREATE or CAUSE

meaning: to support or form the basis of something
example: Free trade agreements underpin much of the global economic order.
wrong: not the same as 'undermine' — underpin SUPPORTS, undermine WEAKENS

title: 🔄 underpin vs undermine — Critical Distinction
body:
These two are frequently confused in IELTS essays:

✅ UNDERPIN = to support from below, to provide a foundation for
'Democratic values underpin this policy.'

❌ UNDERMINE = to weaken gradually, to erode the foundation of
'Corruption undermines democratic institutions.'

Memory trick: Under-PIN = PIN it up (support)
Under-MINE = dig a MINE underneath (weaken the foundation)

quick.label: underpin = support, form the basis of

instruction: Match each verb to its correct meaning:

pairs.meaning: give rise to a feeling or condition
provide the foundation or basis for

explanation: These four verbs describe CAUSATION and SUPPORT at an advanced academic level. Using them precisely replaces vague phrases like 'cause', 'create', 'support', 'weaken' — instantly elevating your Lexical Resource score.

meaning: too large or too small in relation to something else; out of proportion
example: The tax burden falls disproportionately on low-income households.
wrong: not the same as 'unequal' — disproportionate refers to a specific RATIO being off

question: Which sentence uses 'disproportionate' most accurately?
options: The government has a disproportionate amount of money.
Climate change has a disproportionate impact on developing nations, despite their minimal contribution to global emissions.
The essay was disproportionate in its arguments.
She felt disproportionate about the decision.
correct: Climate change has a disproportionate impact on developing nations, despite their minimal contribution to global emissions.
explanation:
'Disproportionate' means the impact is OUT OF PROPORTION to a related measure.

✅ Developing nations contribute little to emissions (small input) but suffer greatly (large impact) — this ratio is disproportionate.

❌ 'Disproportionate amount of money' — requires a comparison (than what?)
❌ 'Disproportionate in its arguments' — arguments aren't measured in quantities
❌ 'Felt disproportionate' — can't use it as a feeling adjective
hint: Disproportionate always implies a comparison — X is too large/small relative to Y.

title: ✏️ Advanced Vocabulary Error
instruction: Find the sentence that misuses an advanced vocabulary word:

sentences.text: Rapid industrialisation precipitated severe environmental degradation throughout the 20th century.
The government's investment in education will undermine economic growth in the long term.
sentences.explanation:
'Undermine' means to WEAKEN — but investment in education SUPPORTS economic growth.

✅ Correct: 'The government's investment in education will underpin economic growth in the long term.'

This is a critical distinction: underpin (support) vs undermine (weaken). Using the wrong one completely reverses your intended meaning.

sentences.text: Globalisation has engendered both unprecedented opportunity and new forms of inequality.
